analysis.one_liner: Bans greenhouse gas emissions from new fossil power plants, fracking, and most oil and gas exports.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to three House committees, never received a hearing or a vote, and died when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would amend the Clean Air Act to make it illegal for any new fossil-fuel power plant to emit greenhouse gases. It would bar federal regulators from approving new LNG export terminals or natural gas pipeline certificates, ban hydraulic fracturing on all U.S. land starting January 1, 2025, and reinstate a ban on exporting domestically produced crude oil and natural gas, with narrow exceptions for trade with Canada and Mexico and for oil exchanges. It was introduced by Rep. Janice Schakowsky and six Democratic cosponsors and never advanced past committee referral.
analysis.who_benefits: Communities living near drilling sites, refineries, and power plants, who bear the brunt of air pollution; younger and future generations, who would face less climate change; and workers in clean-energy industries, whose products would face less fossil-fuel competition. The bill's findings call for a just transition with union training and access to clean-energy jobs for displaced fossil fuel workers.

how_it_helps.text: It prohibits any greenhouse gas emission from new electric utility steam generating units, meaning no new coal- or gas-fired power plant could operate once the bill became law.

It bans hydraulic fracturing on all onshore and offshore land in the United States, effective January 1, 2025, which would stop drilling that releases methane and pollutes air and water near drilling sites.

It reinstates a ban on exports of domestically produced crude oil and natural gas, including LNG, with exceptions for exchanges, temporary transport exports, and historical trade with Canada and Mexico — keeping more domestic fuel production tied to domestic supply.

It bars the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission from approving new LNG terminal applications or natural gas pipeline certificates, unless an approval would actually reduce greenhouse gas emissions at that terminal.

The bill's findings state that fossil fuel use disproportionately damages frontline environmental justice communities and call for transitioning away from fossil fuels with union training and access to clean-energy jobs for workers.

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas companies, coal and gas power plant developers, LNG terminal and pipeline builders, and crude and natural gas exporters would lose major markets and operations. Communities and workers dependent on those industries would face job losses unless the promised just-transition programs were funded. Consumers could face higher energy prices if domestic supply tightened after the fracking and export bans took effect.
analysis.who_pays_short: Fossil fuel producers and energy workers

drawbacks.text: A nationwide fracking ban would eliminate oil and gas production jobs in states like Texas, North Dakota, and Pennsylvania and cut off a major domestic energy source, and the bill creates no funded transition program for those workers — it only states findings calling for a just transition.

Restricting new LNG terminals and banning crude and natural gas exports could raise domestic energy prices for consumers if supply tightened, and would disrupt a natural gas export industry that had grown after Congress lifted the crude export ban in 2015 (the bill amends that 2015 law).

The ban on new fossil power plants applies to any new generating unit regardless of local reliability needs, which could complicate grid planning in regions heavily dependent on gas generation, and the bill pairs no renewable energy build-out requirement with the restrictions.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's climate and public-health benefits would be real and long-term, but it is a blunt instrument: it bans activities outright rather than pricing or regulating them, offers no concrete funding for the fossil fuel workers and communities it says deserve a just transition, and could raise consumer energy prices and disrupt trade relationships. A more gradual or compensated transition would carry lower costs, but the bill as written concentrates the burden on energy-producing regions.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to three House committees — Energy and Commerce, Natural Resources, and Foreign Affairs — none of which took it up, and it expired when the Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Rep. Janice Schakowsky introduced the bill on September 17, 2020, near the end of the 116th Congress, with five additional Democratic cosponsors.
The bill was referred to the Energy and Commerce, Natural Resources, and Foreign Affairs committees; the action record shows no hearing, markup, or floor action after referral.
With only 6 cosponsors out of 231 House Democrats and no committee action, the bill died without a vote when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas producers, LNG and pipeline developers, and exporters of crude and natural gas are better off because the bill never advanced; their operations, markets, and export licenses remain untouched. Households in energy-producing regions also avoided potential job and price impacts.

industries.industry: Oil and gas producers and fracking operators
industries.note: The bill would ban hydraulic fracturing nationwide starting in 2025 and prohibit most crude oil and natural gas exports, eliminating a large share of U.S. oil and gas output and revenue. The industry's interest in the bill ran against the public health and climate benefits supporters claimed.

FERC would be barred from approving new LNG terminal sitings and most natural gas pipeline certificates, freezing planned projects. Communities near proposed terminals would avoid new pollution sources.
No new fossil-fuel steam generating unit could emit greenhouse gases in any quantity, blocking construction of new coal and gas plants. Renewable generators would face less competition.

industries.industry: Crude oil and natural gas exporters
industries.note: The bill reverses the 2015 lifting of the crude export ban and bars natural gas and LNG exports except for narrow trade and transport exceptions, ending a major export business.

Blocking new fossil plants, fracking, and exports would push electricity generation and heating toward renewables, expanding their market. The bill's stated transition framework envisions union clean-energy jobs.
